facts.claim: The title track "Black Powder Soul" was written by Taylor McCall and Dave Pahanish.
Sean McConnell produced the song and the album.
The vinyl release credits recording at Silent Desert Studio in Nolensville, TN, mixing at Dockside Studio, and mastering at Magic Garden Mastering.
McCall says the title song was the hardest he ever wrote, taking three days.
McCall says he had the verses and described the song to his friend Dave Pahanish, who responded with the phrase 'Black Powder Soul'.
McCall and McConnell met for the first time at a co-write that produced 'So Damn Lucky'. The album was made over two weeks in McConnell's home studio.
McCall's own description of the album: a circle of life in which the things that clutter the pure soul are all present, and everyone has a black powder soul that can explode but can also be redeemed.
The album opens with a 49-second clip of McCall's late grandfather and his teenage mother, who were in a traveling gospel group, singing the hymn 'Old Ship of Zion'.
A review describes the title track as opening with a lone reverbed guitar and backing vocal before McCall's whiskey-soaked vocals come in.

The album was released 24 September 2021 on Black Powder Soul Records, marketed and distributed by Thirty Tigers. McCall is from Easley, South Carolina, and now lives in Franklin, Tennessee. His follow-up, 'Mellow War', is stylistically very different.

research.lineage: A dark, gospel-tinged Americana and country record that Holler places among the edgier, good-versus-evil strains of country and compares to Steve Earle.

draft:
The only friend the narrator of **Black Powder Soul** admits to is a gun. "That's why my over under is my only friend," Taylor McCall sings, and the phrase does double work. An over-under is a stacked double-barrel shotgun. It's also a betting line, which fits a man who quit poker after something went wrong in Spokane. The first verse sets him up like a figure from an old ballad: a soldier with no war to fight, a man outside the law, trading in moonshine and bathtub gin. It plays as bragging until that last line. All the swagger lands on loneliness.

The chorus is where the pride splits open. "My heart is burning / My blood runs cold" isn't a contradiction the song tries to settle. He's hot and cold at once, storm clouds overhead and fire underfoot, and the title names what that makes him: black powder, the old unstable stuff that sits quiet until a spark finds it. McCall has described the album as a circle in which everyone carries a soul like that, one that can explode but can also be redeemed. This song keeps the first half of that promise and holds back the second. By the second verse there "ain't no running east or west," and the hustlers and blood money close in like weather.

McCall has said it was the hardest song to write, three days of work. The verses came first. When McCall described the song to co-writer Dave Pahanish, Pahanish answered with the phrase "Black Powder Soul." A man this boxed in by his own story needed somebody else to name it.

Sean McConnell produced, and the album was made over two weeks in his home studio. The song opens on a lone guitar and a backing vocal before McCall comes in. The band then works patiently: a clean electric guitar picking out arpeggios, bass holding the root, a slow, relaxed groove with the snare cracking on the backbeat, and a second guitar laying a sustained, distorted line underneath like smoke. The voice is mid-range with a rasp at the edges, recorded dry and close, and it pushes harder as the drums and that dirty guitar fill in.

Holler compares McCall to Steve Earle and places the record among the edgier, good-versus-evil strains of country, and the inheritance is plain: an outlaw self-portrait that's half confession. The album opens with McCall's late grandfather and mother, singers in a traveling gospel group, on "Old Ship of Zion," and this song answers that hymn from the sinner's side.

It sticks because it puts you inside a man who is burning and freezing at once, proud of the danger in himself and afraid of it, and it never tells you where the spark will land.

factCheck.claim: Narrator's only friend is a gun; the lyric 'That's why my over under is my only friend'
factCheck.note: Quote matches the lyrics exactly. Reading the over-under as a shotgun and a betting term is interpretation of the lyric. Kept, with the extra gun-description detail trimmed.

factCheck.claim: He quit poker after something went wrong in Spokane
factCheck.note: The lyric says only 'I don't play poker since that stint in Spokane'. 'Something went wrong' is unsupported, so it now follows the lyric.

factCheck.claim: Trading in moonshine and bathtub gin
factCheck.note: The lyrics say the Spokane stint was 'over some bootleg moonshine / over my bathtub gin'. Nothing says he traded in them. Reworded.
